content: 1. If a woman does not wish to conceive again, provide her with detailed information about the importance of family planning and available contraceptive options. 2. If the woman expresses interest, connect her with peer support groups, women’s organizations, or community services that can offer additional emotional and practical support. 3. If the woman discloses experiences of violence or if you observe unexplained bruises or injuries that raise suspicion of abuse, refer to the appropriate guidelines for managing such cases (e.g., H4). 4. During follow-up visits, provide advice and counseling tailored to the woman’s condition and needs. 5. If a threatened abortion occurs and bleeding stops, reassure the woman that it is safe to continue the pregnancy and provide standard antenatal care as per established protocols (C1-C18). 6. If bleeding persists, assess and manage the situation according to the guidelines for bleeding in early pregnancy or post-abortion care (B18-B22). If there are signs of infection, such as fever, foul-smelling vaginal discharge, or abdominal pain, administer the first dose of appropriate intravenous or intramuscular antibiotics immediately (B15). 7. For antenatal care, always begin with a rapid assessment and management (RAM) to identify any emergency or priority signs (B3-B7). If no such signs are present, proceed with routine antenatal care. 8. Use the pregnancy status and birth plan chart (C2) to evaluate the woman’s current pregnancy status, history of previous pregnancies, and any general danger signs. Based on this assessment, determine the most appropriate place for delivery and prepare a comprehensive birth and emergency plan. Review and update this plan at every follow-up visit. 9. Screen all pregnant women for pre-eclampsia, anemia, syphilis, and HIV status during antenatal visits, following the respective charts (C3-C6). If any abnormal signs are identified, classify the condition and provide appropriate treatment using the relevant guidelines (C7-C11). 10. Offer preventive measures as indicated (C12), develop a birth and emergency plan (C14-C15), and provide counseling on nutrition (C13), family planning (C16), labor signs, danger signs (C15), and the importance of routine and follow-up visits (C17). Use information and counseling sheets (M1-M19) to support these discussions. 11. Record all findings, including positive observations, the birth plan, treatments provided, and the next scheduled visit, in the home-based maternal card or clinic recording form. 12. During the first antenatal visit, assess the duration of pregnancy, the woman’s expected delivery date, and her age. Ask about her obstetric history, including the number of previous pregnancies, complications such as pre-eclampsia, prior cesarean sections, or other interventions, and any history of stillbirths or neonatal deaths. 13. Evaluate lifestyle factors, such as tobacco, alcohol, or drug use, and exposure to secondhand smoke. Provide appropriate advice on cessation if necessary. 14. For women with a history of cesarean delivery, age under 14 years, transverse lie, multiple pregnancies, or other high-risk factors, explain the need for delivery at a referral-level facility and develop a detailed birth and emergency plan. 15. Screen for pre-eclampsia at every visit by measuring blood pressure and assessing for symptoms such as severe headaches or visual disturbances. If severe pre-eclampsia is diagnosed, administer magnesium sulfate and antihypertensive medications, revise the birth plan, and refer the woman urgently to a hospital. 16. For anemia, assess hemoglobin levels and look for clinical signs such as pallor. Treat severe anemia with a double dose of iron supplements, counsel on compliance, and follow up within two weeks. Refer to a hospital if necessary. 17. Test all pregnant women for syphilis at the first visit using the rapid plasma reagin (RPR) test. If positive, treat with benzathine benzylpenicillin or erythromycin (if allergic) and plan to treat the newborn. Encourage the woman to bring her partner for treatment and counsel on safer sex practices. 18. Test all pregnant women for HIV at the first antenatal visit and provide counseling on the implications of the results. If HIV-positive, initiate antiretroviral therapy (ART), support adherence, and refer to HIV services for further care. Counsel on family planning, infant feeding options, and safer sex practices. 19. If the woman refuses HIV testing or does not disclose her status, assess for signs of advanced HIV infection, counsel on safer sex, and encourage partner testing. 20. If there is no fetal movement, assess the situation by feeling for fetal movements and listening for the fetal heart. If the baby is likely deceased, inform the woman and her partner sensitively and refer to a hospital. 21. If membranes have ruptured without labor, assess for signs of infection, such as fever or foul-smelling discharge. Administer appropriate antibiotics and corticosteroids if preterm birth is imminent, and refer urgently to a hospital. 22. For all antenatal care visits, ensure comprehensive assessment, counseling, and management tailored to the woman’s individual needs and clinical findings.
